outcomes: Say that sounds are made when things shake or vibrate.
Name the ear as the body part we use to hear.
Sort sounds into loud and quiet.
Describe the sounds we hear around us.
Listen carefully and identify different sounds.

concepts.title: Sounds All Around Us
concepts.explanation:
There are sounds everywhere, all the time — but we are usually too busy to notice them.

Sit somewhere and stay very still. Close your eyes and just listen. Wait quietly and listen hard for a whole minute.

Now think about what you heard. Maybe a bird calling. Maybe a goat. Maybe the wind moving, a car passing, or people talking somewhere nearby.

Count the different sounds on your fingers. You probably heard more than you expected.

Here is the surprising part: even when a place feels quiet, there are still little sounds to hear. Quiet does not mean there is no sound at all — it just means the sounds are small and soft.

Good scientists notice things. Listening carefully is one of the best ways to notice the world.
concepts.example: Close your eyes and listen for one whole minute. Then count on your fingers how many different sounds you heard, and name each one.

concepts.title: How We Make Sounds
concepts.explanation:
Here is the big science idea of this unit: sounds happen when things shake.

When something moves back and forth very fast, it makes a sound. That fast shaking has a special name — vibrating.

Stretch a rubber band between your fingers and pluck it gently. Look closely. You can see it shaking, so fast that it blurs. That shaking is the vibration, and that is what makes the sound you hear.

Now tap a metal pot with a spoon. You hear a sound. Rest your finger gently on the pot while it is still ringing — you can feel it buzzing. The pot is vibrating too.

Try one more. Put your fingers gently on the front of your throat and hum. Can you feel the buzzing under your fingers? That is your voice vibrating inside you.

Every single sound, everywhere, comes from something shaking and moving.
concepts.example: Put your fingers on your throat and hum a long note. Say what you can feel, and use the science word for that fast shaking.

concepts.title: Loud Sounds and Quiet Sounds
concepts.explanation:
Sounds come in different sizes. Some sounds are loud, and some sounds are quiet. Quiet sounds are sometimes called soft sounds.

The good news is that you can control how loud or quiet a sound is.

Clap your hands very softly. That is a quiet clap. Now clap firmly — but not near anyone's ears. That is a loud clap. You made both, using the same two hands.

Try it with your voice. Whisper a word very quietly. Now say the same word in your normal voice. Same word, different loudness.

Try it with a pot. Bang it firmly and it makes a loud sound. Tap it lightly and it makes a quiet one.

What makes the difference? How much energy you give it. A bigger, harder movement makes a bigger vibration, and a bigger vibration makes a louder sound.
concepts.example: Clap once quietly and once loudly. Say which one needed more energy from you, and why it sounded louder.

concepts.title: How We Hear With Our Ears
concepts.explanation:
You hear with your ears. You have two of them, one on each side of your head — and there is a good reason for that.

Touch your ears now, one on each side.

Your ears are shaped a little like small cups, and they catch sounds travelling through the air. Try cupping your hands behind your ears and listening. Sounds get a bit louder, because your hands are catching even more sound.

Now here is why two ears are so useful. Close your eyes and ask someone to make a soft sound on your left side, then on your right side. Each time, point to where the sound came from.

You can do it because a sound from the left reaches your left ear a tiny bit sooner and a tiny bit louder. Your brain notices that difference and works out which direction the sound came from. Two ears help you find where a sound is.

Cover your ears with your hands and the sound becomes quiet and far away, because your hands are blocking it.
concepts.example: Close your eyes while someone makes a soft sound to one side of you. Point to where it came from, then say why two ears helped you.

concepts.title: Sounds Travel, and We Keep Ears Safe
concepts.explanation:
Sound has to travel to reach you. It moves through the air, from the thing that is shaking all the way to your ears.

Here is how you can tell. Ask someone to clap from far across the room, then clap again standing close to you. The close clap sounds louder.

That is because sound gets weaker as it travels. The further a sound has to go, the quieter it is when it arrives. A sound made far away reaches you faint and small.

Now the important part: looking after your ears. Your ears are delicate, and very loud sounds can hurt them. Once hearing is damaged, it does not always come back.

So keep loud noises away from your ears. Do not shout right into someone's ear, and do not let anyone shout into yours. If a sound is so loud that it hurts, cover your ears with your hands and move away from it.

Your ears let you hear a bird singing, your mother's voice, and someone reciting beautifully. They are worth protecting.
concepts.example: Ask someone to clap far away and then close to you. Say which was louder and why. Then say one way you will keep your ears safe.
